newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: FEATURE-U.K. links fondly pursued in Bangladesh.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.K. links fondly pursued in Bangladesh.

text.p: Fifty years after the British left what now is Bangladesh, the bond between the former colonial rulers and their former subjects in this northeastern tea-growing district seems to be getting stronger every day.
"The friendship between us and Britain is ever-lasting," said Abdus Sattar, a journalist in Sylhet, which has given Britain many of the 300,000 Bangladeshis now living there.
The urge for closer ties was expressed more concretely last week when Prince Charles, heir to the British thorne, turned on an earth satellite station in Sylhet built by British Telecom.

The people of Sylhet boast a special relationship with Britain and say the ties will never diminish. "The bridge of friendship between Sylhet and the U.K. has been a permanent feature, and can't be demolished," Sattar said.
The former East Pakistan was part of imperial British India until Britain withdrew in 1947.
The satellite station will provide better communications between Sylhet and England, and has fulfilled a long-time desire, said Bangladesh Telecommunications Minister Mohammad Nasim.
Charles' father, Prince Philip, also visited Sylhet 14 years ago, and most other British dignitaries seem to find time to visit here when in Bangladesh.
Sylhet natives comprise one of the biggest emigrant communities in Britain. "Maybe the oldest too," said Sattar, who has several relatives settled permanently in Britain.

Robert Lindsay, an official of the British East India Co that created the British Raj, or administration, on the subcontinent, wrote in his biography that Sylhet native Syed Ali came to London in 1809.
FIRST VISITOR?
"He (Ali) was probably the first visitor to England from the subcontinent," said Sattar who did research for the biography.

Ali had cooked for Lindsay when he was posted here as local administrator, and later went to London and sought out his employer. How Ali reached London is not known, but many believe he worked out his passage on a foreign ship, and escaped.
Hundreds of thousands of other Sylhetis have since used a variety of means and routes to get to England.
While British-bashing by politicians and intellectuals still is common in the region, Sylhet residents look back fondly on the old colonial days.
"It seems people here, since their childhood, aim to settle in England," said Ahmed Shamim, a local youth. "They think Britain (is) their second home."

Said Nargis Islam, a social worker in Sylhet whose daughter lives in London: "Ninety percent of the families in Sylhet have one or more relatives living in Britain. Many live on what their London-living son, brother and uncle send home."

Sylhet natives now have established themselves in British society and business. Some 10,000 Indian restaurants there are owned by the Sylhetis with annual turnover reaching 1.5 billion sterling. They employ more than 60,000 people, mostly Bangladeshis.
The money Sylhetis send back to Bangladesh is a major part of the estimated $1.2 billion annual remittances from workers.
Britain recognises the growing influence of Sylhetis as they slowly make their way into politics and the economy.

British Telecom installed the Sylhet earth satellite at its own cost, but knowing it would pay them in huge telephone bills. Some 138,826 calls were made between Sylhet and London in January alone, local telecom officials said.
POLITICAL CLOUT
"People of Sylheti origin enjoy significant political clout in some areas in Britain," said lawyer Azizul Mailk Chowdhury.
Candidates in Oldham, Birmingham, Manchestar and East London need the support of Sylheti people to win elections.

"That's one of the reasons why British leaders visit Sylhet whenever they come to Bangladesh. Sometimes they come to Bangladesh only to visit Sylhet and earn the sympathy of electorates from Sylheti community," Chowdhury told Reuters.
But not everybody in Sylhet likes its British connection.

"It's creating a social imbalance and thus tension in the society. Neither everybody can go to London nor everyone receive money from there. So one can easily feel the disparity between the rich and the poor," said Ahmed Shamim.
"The cost of living in Sylhet is probably the highest in Bangladesh because of the constant inflow of remittances. Those who don't have money flowing in (from Britain) suffer badly."
